Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- 31-year-old with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, sore, erythematous dermatitis with xerosis/fissuring, affecting chest, hands, and antecubital fossae; no systemic features; sleep and function significantly impacted. Past eczema; past asthma (resolved). OTC topical steroid and antihistamines provided little benefit to date.
- Most likely: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare—consistent with history, distribution (flexures/hands/trunk), severe itch, xerosis, and clinician’s visual impression.
- Consider: Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis—acute onset after recent hiking and possible exposures; patient denies product changes.
- Consider: Scabies—severe nocturnal pruritus and shared housing; no classic burrows reported.
- Plan aligns with eczema management: prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid and regular emollients; trial a stronger antihistamine; trigger diary; review in 7–10 days, sooner if worsening.
- Distribution note: Patient reports chest/hands/flexures; clinician also mentioned back involvement (conflict noted).

Management Plan
- Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid (specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Emollients for bathing/showering and regular skin moisturization (product and frequency not documented).
- Antihistamine: Fexofenadine trial (dose/frequency not documented); prior OTC antihistamines provided little relief.
- Trigger diary: track potential irritants/allergens (e.g., soaps, detergents, clothing, environmental exposures).
- Safety/worsening advice: return if no improvement or if signs of infection develop (e.g., pus, spreading erythema, fever) or if household contacts become itchy (to reassess for scabies/contact dermatitis).
- Follow-up: in about 1 week if not improving.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare – High likelihood: Prior eczema, flexural/hand/trunk involvement, severe pruritus with xerosis/fissuring, clinician impression consistent.
- Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood: Acute onset; hands/chest distribution plausible; recent hiking; denies new products.
- Scabies – Moderate likelihood: Severe itch interfering with sleep and shared living; absence of classic signs does not exclude early scabies.
